description: We are a team of 5 with the goal of helping differently abled people visualize how earth feels like through sound.
summary:
THESOUND.EARTH is an interactive Earth Information Jukebox that transforms NASA Earth science data into music, turning the planet's changing systems into an experience people can both see and hear. By combining NASA PO.DAAC OSCAR ocean-current measurements with NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) visualizations, it translates planetary processes such as ocean circulation, temperature changes, atmospheric movement and shifting ice coverage into musical elements including rhythm, melody, pitch and harmony. These compositions are paired with an interactive 3D Earth globe, synchronized visualizations and an auditable sonification system that connects musical events to their underlying scientific measurements or visual features.
Our aim is to make Earth science more accessible, engaging and inclusive by introducing sound as a new way to explore and understand our planet. With narration and accessible navigation for differently abled and visually impaired users, THESOUND.EARTH transforms complex scientific information into an immersive educational experience, helping students, educators and the public discover environmental patterns and develop a deeper connection with our changing planet.
details:
THESOUND.EARTH — Hear the Music of Earth

THESOUND.EARTH is an interactive Earth Information Jukebox that transforms NASA ocean-current data and SVS visualizations into music. By combining scientific data sonification, an interactive 3D globe and NASA Earth visualizations, it allows people to both see and hear how our planet's oceans move and change.

The music is an artistic encoding of real satellite-derived scientific measurements. It is not a recording of the ocean or the natural sounds of underwater environments. Instead, the Earth's physical processes directly influence the rhythm, pitch, harmony and intensity of the composition.

How It Works

THESOUND.EARTH uses daily ocean surface-current measurements from NASA's PO.DAAC OSCAR (Ocean Surface Current Analysis Real-time) dataset, accessed through NASA Earthdata. The dataset provides measurements at 0.25° spatial resolution.

The project focuses on the Gulf Stream region (30–40°N, 60–80°W) and analyses available data from 2021–2026.

Scientific measurements are translated into musical elements through a deterministic sonification system, meaning that the same data and random seed always produce the same musical composition.

1. Drums and Rhythm: Current Speed

The 95th-percentile surface current speed (p95) determines the intensity and density of the percussion.

  • Slow-moving water produces a light kick drum.
  • Faster currents introduce snares and shakers.
  • The strongest currents trigger additional percussion fills.

As ocean currents accelerate or weaken, the rhythm changes accordingly.

2. Harmony: Ocean Current Direction

The harmonic structure is influenced by the ageostrophic component of ocean currents, which represents the flow not explained by geostrophic balance and is largely influenced by wind-driven processes.

Its direction determines the chord progression in D minor:

  • East: D minor (Dm).
  • North: B-flat major (B♭).
  • West: G minor (Gm).
  • South: C major (C).

A hysteresis system prevents small fluctuations from causing unnatural chord changes. A new chord must be indicated for two consecutive bars before the progression changes.

3. Harmonic Holds: Periods of Weak Flow

When the ageostrophic component falls below 0.013 m/s, the existing chord is sustained rather than introducing a new one. This creates periods of harmonic stillness that represent relatively weak ocean flow.

4. Bass: Chord Foundation

The bass follows the root note of the currently active chord, providing a consistent harmonic foundation for the composition.

5. Musical Structure

Each composition follows five stages that reflect the development of the underlying data:

  • Intro: Introduces the musical theme.
  • Build: Develops the rhythm and harmonic movement.
  • Peak: Represents periods of stronger activity.
  • Calm: Introduces softer dynamics and sustained harmonies.
  • Outro: Brings the composition to a close.

The audio is rendered using FluidSynth and a licensed SoundFont, producing a multi-track musical composition.

Scientific Transparency: Each musical bar represents a block of days and corresponds directly to a row in the public audit_table.json. This allows users to trace the music back to the exact scientific measurements and calculations that generated it.

Missing measurements are treated as rests, never as zero values. This ensures that unavailable scientific data is not misrepresented.

How to Use THESOUND.EARTH

  1. Access the Platform: Visit https://thesound.earth to open the THESOUND.EARTH application.
  2. Select Accessibility Preferences: Choose whether to enable voice assistance according to your preference.
  3. Choose a Geographical Region: Explore the interactive 3D globe and click on the geographical region you wish to experience through music.
  4. Explore the Scientific Information: Once a region is selected, the left-side evidence panel and right-side detail panel display relevant scientific observations, measurements and contextual information. Explore both panels to understand the environmental characteristics of your selected region.
  5. Explore NASA SVS Visualizations: Navigate to the NASA SVS tab and search or browse the available NASA Earth science visualizations. Select the visualization you wish to explore.
  6. Pair the Visualization: Click Pair Visual to connect your selected NASA visualization with the chosen geographical region and its scientific information.
  7. Generate Sound: Click Generate Sound to create the corresponding musical composition based on the available scientific data and paired visualization.

The resulting experience combines scientific evidence, NASA visualizations, interactive 3D exploration and music, allowing users to experience Earth's processes through both sight and sound.

Accessibility for Blind and Low-Vision Users

Accessibility is a fundamental part of THESOUND.EARTH. The platform aims to make Earth science exploration possible without depending entirely on visual information.

Narration Mode

Users can enable narration to hear spoken descriptions of each musical section, including current speed, direction and chord progression. This provides scientific context while the music plays.

Voice-Assisted Navigation

Voice commands allow users to control playback, select geographical regions and time periods, and ask questions about the currently playing composition.

Keyboard and Screen-Reader Navigation

Application controls are designed to support keyboard interaction and screen readers, allowing users to explore the experience without requiring a mouse.

Accessible Descriptions

Every musical section includes a text description explaining the scientific activity represented by the composition.

Why It Matters

Earth science is often communicated through satellite images, maps, graphs and numerical datasets. Although these methods are valuable, they can make complex environmental processes difficult to access, particularly for blind and visually impaired individuals.

THESOUND.EARTH introduces sound as another way to explore scientific information. By translating ocean movements and changing current conditions into musical patterns, the platform makes environmental data more engaging and accessible to blind and low-vision users, students, educators and the wider public.

It also offers a new way for anyone to recognise patterns in Earth's behaviour through rhythm, harmony and sound, complementing conventional scientific visualizations.

Scientific Accuracy and Limitations

THESOUND.EARTH prioritizes scientific transparency and does not claim that its generated music represents the actual sounds of the ocean.

  • The music is an artistic encoding of scientific measurements, not a natural ocean recording.
  • The ageostrophic component has a median magnitude of approximately 0.02 m/s. Its chord mapping is an artistic sonification choice, not a scientific conclusion about musical relationships in ocean circulation.
  • The available 2026 dataset ends at the latest date for which PO.DAAC data had been released when the dataset was downloaded.
  • The final data block of a year may contain fewer than seven days.
  • Missing or unavailable measurements produce rests rather than fabricated values.
  • All musical mappings follow documented and reproducible rules.

The public audit table provides transparency into the relationship between the original measurements and the generated music.

Technology and Data Sources

Programming and Backend: Python, FastAPI, Starlette, Uvicorn and Node.js.

Scientific Processing: NumPy, Mido and scientific data-processing libraries.

Music Generation: FluidSynth and licensed SoundFont synthesis.

Video Processing: FFmpeg and ImageIO.

3D Visualization: Three.js and WebGL, including custom shaders and dynamic Earth rendering.

Audio Technology: Web Audio API, multi-channel spatialization and FFT-based audio spectrum analysis.

Performance: Web Workers, GPU acceleration, asynchronous processing and HTTP 206 Byte-Range streaming.

Scientific Data Sources: NASA PO.DAAC OSCAR, NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) and NASA Earth Information Center (EIC).

Project Website: https://thesound.earth

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/nullkai-empt/thesound.earth

AI Use and Credits: Antigravity AI assisted with code development and automated testing.
